title: Curriculum Vitae — Simen Kvaal
text:
Associate Professor of Theoretical Chemistry
Department of Chemistry, University of Oslo
Academic website: University of Oslo profile
ORCID: 0000-0002-5118-4546


Theoretical and computational quantum chemistry, with emphasis on coupled-cluster theory, density-functional theory, quantum dynamics, and mathematical and numerical analysis of electronic-structure methods. Research at the interface of chemistry, physics, applied mathematics, and quantum computing.



2024–present — Associate Professor in Theoretical Chemistry
Department of Chemistry, University of Oslo
2015–2024 — Scientific Researcher
Hylleraas Centre for Quantum Molecular Sciences, University of Oslo
(previously the Centre for Theoretical and Computational Chemistry)
2012–2015 — Scientific Researcher
Centre for Theoretical and Computational Chemistry (CTCC), University of Oslo
ERC Advanced Grant project ABACUS, PI: Trygve Helgaker
2010–2011 — Postdoctoral Fellow
Department of Mathematics, Universität Tübingen, Germany
On leave from the University of Oslo. Supervisor: Prof. Christian Lubich
2009–2011 — Postdoctoral Fellow
Centre of Mathematics for Applications, University of Oslo
2008–2009 — Researcher
Centre of Mathematics for Applications, University of Oslo


2006–2007 — Developer/Researcher, Faster Imaging AS (10% part-time)
Image-compression techniques.
2001 and 2002 — Developer, Simula Research Laboratory (summer employment)
Integration of large-scale eigenvalue solvers in Diffpack (C++ finite-element library); scripts for translating large LaTeX documents to HTML.




2009 — PhD, University of Oslo
Centre of Mathematics for Applications / Department of Physics
Thesis: Analysis of many-body methods for quantum dots
Supervisors: Morten Hjorth-Jensen (main), Ragnar Winther (co-supervisor)
2004 — MSc (cand. scient.), University of Oslo
Department of Physics
Thesis: A critical study of the finite difference and finite element methods for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (Grade A)
Supervisors: Morten Hjorth-Jensen (main), Hans Petter Langtangen (co-supervisor)












Year
Role
Programme / project
Funding




2025
Partner
RCN Centre for Quantum Technology — Center for Quantum Computing and Applications (QSTAR), leader: Franz Fuchs; project period 2026–2029
NOK 60M (€5.6M)


2022
Co-PI
RCN Large Interdisciplinary Researcher Project — Mathematics for quantum computation and many-body theory (QOMBINE)
NOK 25M (€2.1M)


2019
PI, with Thomas Bondo Pedersen
Centre for Advanced Study — Attosecond Quantum Dynamics Beyond the Born-Oppenheimer Approximation (ATTODYN); academic year 2021/22 plus one-year COVID-19 extension
NOK 3.4M (€0.3M)


2018
Collaborator
Peder Sather Center for Advanced Study Grant — A posteriori error estimates for coupled-cluster theory
USD 22k (€20k)


2015
Collaborator
Peder Sather Center for Advanced Study Grant — Advanced Computational Methods for the Quantum Mechanical Many-Body Problem in Physics and Quantum Chemistry
USD 25k (€23k)


2014–2021
PI
ERC Starting Grant — Bivariational Approximations in Quantum Mechanics and Applications to Quantum Chemistry (BIVAQUM)
€1.5M












TipBibliographical summary — 11 September 2026



48 peer-reviewed journal articles in mathematics, physics, and chemistry
1 published book chapter
6 single-author papers (2008–2023)
1,835 citations · h-index 22







2025–present — KJM5600/9600, Quantum Chemistry (MSc/PhD level)
Course administrator and lecturer (100% of course), Department of Chemistry, University of Oslo.
2024–present — KJM2601, Quantum Chemistry and Spectroscopy (BSc level)
Course administrator and lecturer (100% of course), Department of Chemistry, University of Oslo.
2015–2017 — FYS-KJM4480, Quantum Mechanics for Many-Particle Systems (MSc/PhD level; 3 semesters)
Course administrator and lecturer (100% of course), Departments of Physics and Chemistry, University of Oslo.
2017 — IN-KJM1900, Introduction to Programming for Chemists
Course administrator and lecturer (50% of course); correction of compulsory assignments, Departments of Informatics and Chemistry, University of Oslo.



2022–present — European Summer School in Quantum Chemistry (ESQC), Sicily
Lecturer on mathematical methods in quantum chemistry (8 hours). Biennial school; head organizer: Trond Saue, University of Toulouse.
2023–present — Annual Hylleraas School
Lecturer electron dynamics, density-functional theory, and practical graphical design.



2005–2006 — INF-MAT3360, Introduction to Partial Differential Equations (2 semesters)
Group tutor; responsible for all student tutoring sessions (4 hours/week) and correction of compulsory assignments, Departments of Informatics and Mathematics, University of Oslo.
2000 — FYS-201, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics (spring semester)
Group tutor; responsible for all student tutoring sessions (4 hours/week), Department of Physics, University of Oslo.




PhD supervision: 4 as main supervisor; 4 as co-supervisor (2 currently active).
MSc supervision: 3 as main supervisor; 5 informal co-supervisions during PhD studies.



Håkon Richard Fredheim, PhD student (2022–2026) — main supervisor; now consultant, Sopra Steria AS.
Snorre Bergan, PhD student (2022–present) — co-supervisor.
Simon E. Schrader, PhD student (2022–2026) — main supervisor; now independent researcher.
Tilmann Bodenstein, postdoctoral researcher (2019–2021) — now researcher at the Hylleraas Centre.
Fabian M. Faulstich, PhD student (2017–2020) — main supervisor; now at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, USA.
Benedicte Ofstad, PhD student (2016–2023) — main supervisor; now at the Institute for Energy Technology.
Rolf H. Myhre, postdoctoral researcher (2016–2018) — now researcher at the Norwegian Meteorological Institute.
Andre Laestadius, postdoctoral researcher (2015–2020) — now Associate Professor at Oslo Metropolitan University.
Gustav Baardsen, PhD student (2011–2014) — co-supervisor; now Research Scientist at Varian, Helsinki.






2025 — WATOC2025, Congress of the World Association of Theoretically Oriented Chemists — member of organizing committee; >1,100 participants.
2023 — Molecular Quantum Dynamics, international workshop, Centre for Advanced Study — initiator and member of four-person organizing committee.
2015 — Fundamental Aspects of DFT, international workshop, Centre for Theoretical and Computational Chemistry — member of two-person organizing committee.
2010 — Time-Dependent Quantum Mechanics — Analysis and Numerics, international workshop, Centre of Mathematics for Applications — initiator and member of three-person organizing committee.





Ludwik Adamowicz, University of Arizona, USA — explicitly correlated Gaussians; quantum chemistry beyond the Born–Oppenheimer approximation.
Fabian Faulstich, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, USA — analysis of coupled-cluster methods.
Elias Jarlebring, KTH, Sweden — numerical analysis for quantum mechanics and chemistry.
Andre Laestadius, OsloMet, Norway — mathematical analysis in quantum chemistry.
Caroline Lasser, Technical University of Munich, Germany — numerical analysis in quantum dynamics.
Reinhold Schneider, Technical University of Berlin, Germany — coupled-cluster theory and tensor-network states.







Co-PI, Research Theme 7: Machine Learning and Mathematical Chemistry, Hylleraas Centre (2023–present).
Member, Programme Council for Chemistry, Department of Chemistry, University of Oslo (2024–present) — advisory body for the chemistry study programmes.
Member, dScience Community Forum, University of Oslo (2020–present).
Member, Young Academy of Norway (2014–2019); membership by application and selection based on academic merit, profile, and diversity.
In-house graphical designer, Hylleraas Centre.
Organized weekly seminars at the Centre for Theoretical and Computational Chemistry (2015).




Referee for journals including Nature, Physical Review Letters, Physical Review A, Physical Review X, Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis, The European Physical Journal, Foundations of Computational Mathematics, International Journal of Quantum Chemistry, The Journal of Chemical Physics, and Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation.

Grant application reviewer for ETH Research and the US National Science Foundation.
External examiner for MSc and BSc students, OsloMet (2021–2022).
Member of mock-interview panels for ERC interview training, University of Oslo (2015–present).





Popular-science writing (2010–2014)
Writer for the popular-science blog Kollokvium.
Radio appearances (2010–2014)
NRK Ekko and Abels Tårn.
Competition judging
Judge for Immunidol, public-outreach competition of the Norwegian Society of Immunology (2013).

Rothe’s Method for Quantum Dynamics in Atoms and Molecules with Gaussian Wavepackets
Simon Elias Schrader, Håkon Emil Kristiansen, Aleksander P. Wozniak, Ludwik Adamowicz, Simen Kvaal, and Thomas Bondo Pedersen (2026). doi:10.48550/arXiv.2606.20947


Abstract


Capable of capturing both bound and continuum quantum dynamics, Gaussian wavepackets are highly attractive basis functions for simulating laser-driven processes in atoms and molecules. Unfortunately, fully flexible Gaussian wavepackets are exceedingly challenging to propagate in a numerically stable manner within the framework of conventional time-dependent variational principles. In this chapter, we discuss the sources of the numerical issues and review an alternative approach, Rothe’s method, that offers a route to improved numerical stability. Recent proof-of-concept simulations based on Rothe’s method indicate that Gaussian wavepackets provide results on par with highly accurate grid-based methods for both electronic and rovibrational quantum dynamics, including ultrafast nonlinear processes that involve the continuum such as high-harmonic generation. Remarkably few Gaussian wavepackets are needed to achieve the high accuracy of grid-based approaches, indicating that further algorithmic developments and efficient implementations may enable efficient simulations of not only electronic and rovibrational phenomena but also fully coupled electronic-nuclear quantum dynamics with significantly reduced memory demands. We also point out remaining practical challenges, including matrix elements of the squared Hamiltonian and the treatment of Coulomb cusps.



Reduced Density Matrix Functional Theory And A Reduced Formulation Of Density Functional Theory
Håkon R. Fredheim and Simen Kvaal (2026). doi:10.48550/arXiv.2510.12242


Abstract


A mathematical framework for reduced density matrix functional theory (RDMFT) is proposed. The work is inspired by and generalizes the work by E.H. Lieb [E.H. Lieb, Int. J. Quant. Chem. 24(1983), pp.243–277] on density-functional theory (DFT). We introduce a Banach space for density matrices with finite kinetic energy. The dual space is a rich class of single-particle potentials, i.e., Hermitian forms. The ground state energy of an \(N\)-fermion system with external forces given by any such Hermitian form is expressed as the Legendre–Fenchel transform of a convex and lower semicontinuous “universal” reduced density matrix functional. The formalism is employed to provide a mathematical framework for density-functional theory (DFT). The main tool here is a rigorous definition of diagonals of reduced density matrices. The result is a refinement of Lieb’s results on DFT applicable to a wide variety of models.






No need for a grid: Adaptive fully-flexible gaussians for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation
Simen Kvaal, Caroline Lasser, Thomas Bondo Pedersen, and Ludwik Adamowicz (2022). arXiv


Abstract


Linear combinations of complex gaussian functions, where the nonlinear parameters are allowed to vary, are shown to be an extremely flexible representation for the solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in one spatial dimension. Propagation of such wavefunctions using the Dirac–Frenkel variational principle is notoriously hard, and we present instead a scheme based on the method of vertical lines, or Rothe’s method. We apply the method to a simple test system mimicking an atom subject to an extreme laser pulse, producing complicated ionization dynamics. The scheme is shown to perform very well on this model. Since the propagation method can be formulated entirely in terms of gaussian integrals and expectation values, we eliminate the need for large grids using only a handful of gaussian functions but with the same accuracy. This paves the way for accurate and affordable solutions of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for multi-atom molecules beyond the Born–Oppenheimer approximation.

title: Some GitHub repositories
text:
Some GitHub repositories
This is a collection of some of my public personal GitHub repositories, with pedagogical, research, or recreational content. Unless otherwise stated, the code is human written.



Repository
Description




GIAOINT
A recent experiment: A Codex/Claude-coded C++ integral code for gauge-including atomic orbitals (GIAOs), also known as London orbitals. These are needed for electronic-structure theory in external uniform magnetic fields. The code is quite efficient and supplies PyBind11 bindings.


fft_tdse
HySE: simulation toolbox for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation dveloped for ease-of-use, aiming for physics and chemistry didactical use, but also reaseach.


dst_tdse
Discrete-sine-transform based solver for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in multiple dimensions.


quarto-canvas
Codex-coded extension for quarto that renders Obsidian canvases in quarto websites.


ultra_fractal_tools
Support for Ultra Fractal formula files in VSCode, including a Codex skill.


Orbitals
Hydrogen orbital visualizer. Coded with Codex. Link to live simulation: Orbitals


FEMDVR
A simple implementation of the Finite Element Discrete Variable Representation method.
